name: Beth Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm line lead on the tablet packing hall at Corvan Pharma, out by the airport. We press tablets for blood pressure medicine and seal them into blister packs, the foil strips you push pills out of. I look after two tablet presses and a blister machine, plus a team of five, in a gown and hairnet all day because it's a clean room. I love that every batch has to be perfect, because someone's gran is taking these. The paperwork is the bit that drags.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much paperwork are we talking?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every batch has a record, every stop has a reason, and if anything's off we write a deviation report, which is basically a formal explanation. I use an AI assistant every day to draft those, then I check and sign them. It's cut the paperwork from an hour a shift to about twenty minutes. I'm also teaching myself a bit of Python in the evenings, just because I like knowing how things work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. That would surprise me, because it's already useful for me. But okay, mostly hype, a bit of time saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a decent tool and leave it there. To friends I'd say the hype was silly but the tools are real, like spellcheck. Online I'd probably just share a meme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. Corvan's growing. Medicines always need making, and I'm good at what I do. The twenty minutes of paperwork I've saved is a nice bonus, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for reports and keep learning Python in the evenings, because it's interesting either way. I'd apply for the automation technician apprenticeship Corvan runs, which comes up every spring. And Hassan (my partner) and I would keep saving about £300 a month for a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a touch disappointed, because I like new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the automation apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, paid, learning to maintain and program the packing machines and robots. Only two places a year. I missed it last year by one place, so I'd go again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else on your mind in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hassan's contract. He does IT support on rolling six-month contracts, so we never quite know. That's there with or without AI.

I'd tell friends the **hype was silly** but the tools are real.
think: Corvan is **growing** and medicines always need making.
The **twenty minutes** saved on paperwork is a bonus, not a threat.
do: Keep using AI to **draft reports** every shift.
Apply again for the **automation apprenticeship** in spring.
Save **£300 a month** with Hassan for a flat.
feel: **Calm**, slightly **disappointed** as someone who likes new things.

fieldNote: She is an **everyday AI user** and sees it as routine.

She missed the **apprenticeship** by one place and would try again.

steps.text: Keep drafting deviation reports with the AI assistant
Reapply for Corvan's automation technician apprenticeship in spring
Save £300 a month with Hassan towards a flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that sounds like where we're going. The office first, the clean room later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is a good time to learn the new systems, because the people who understand them will be fine. To friends I'd say it's not doom, it's a reshuffle. I'd post the odd thing about my Python projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not worried for me. I'm worried for my partner Hassan, because IT support is answering questions and fixing logins. That's exactly the stuff on that card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard for the automation apprenticeship and, if I missed it again, pay for a robotics course myself, about £1,200. I'd help Hassan look at moving into hands-on IT, like installing kit in factories. And we'd keep saving, maybe bump it to £400.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Hassan, quite excited for myself, which is an odd mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you bring that up with Hassan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gently. He gets defensive about work. I'd probably show him a job ad for factory systems installers and say, look, you'd be good at this, rather than say his job's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'reshuffle'. Who loses out in a reshuffle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who can't or won't move. On my team, Joyce is 61 and hates screens. I'd try to get her into training, but honestly, I don't know if she'd go.

say: I'd say people who **learn the systems** now will be fine.
I'd tell friends it's a **reshuffle**, not doom.
think: I'm **not worried** about my own job.
My partner Hassan's **IT support** job is exactly what's on the card.
do: Push for the **apprenticeship** or pay £1,200 for a robotics course.
Help Hassan look at **hands-on IT** work in factories.
S1.quote: I'm not worried for me. I'm worried for my partner Hassan, because IT support is answering questions and fixing logins.
fieldNote: Her own job feels safe; the **household risk** is her partner's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking stuff. Hassan's job goes then. And mine in 2031. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we should be learning everything about the robots now, because we'll be the ones setting them up. To friends I'd say get practical, get a skill that needs hands. I'd be quite blunt about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's both of us. My partner's helpdesk job is gone by 2028, and my packing line goes around 2031. That's our whole household income in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the robotics course right away and pay for it myself. I'd use the AI tools to learn faster, every evening. Hassan and I would stop saving for a flat and keep the money liquid, and we'd look at moving to a cheaper town near the big pharma parks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I'm normally the one who's excited by change, but two years is too fast for anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move near the pharma parks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if there are robot technician jobs anywhere, it'll be where the big plants are. There's a cluster up north with six plants within ten miles. Better odds than one plant by the airport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Joyce?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To take whatever redundancy deal she can get and retire early, if the numbers work. I'd hate saying it, but she's 61 and two years isn't enough to retrain.

say: I'd tell colleagues to **learn the robots** now, because we'll set them up.
I'd tell friends to get a **hands-on skill**, bluntly.
think: My **packing line** goes around 2031, so both incomes go within five years.
do: Start the **robotics course** right away, self-funded.
Pause the **flat savings** and keep cash available.
Look at **moving north** near a cluster of pharma plants.
feel: **Alarmed**, even as someone who usually **likes change**.
S2.quote: My partner's helpdesk job is gone by 2028, and my packing line goes around 2031. That's our whole household income in five years.
fieldNote: Her adaptability doesn't calm her because **both incomes** are at risk.
She'd **move region** to improve her odds of a technician job.
She'd advise an older colleague to **retire early**.

steps.text: Pay for the robotics course and start it this month
Study robot programming every evening with AI tutors
Pause flat savings and keep the cash easy to reach
Move north near the cluster of six pharma plants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. Okay, that's much more workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we've got time, so let's make a plan and stick to it. To friends I'd say five years is plenty if you start now. I'd probably start a little group at work for people who want to learn the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I can get into robotics before 2034 easily. I'd still be a bit worried, mostly because my partner Hassan tends to put things off. He has until 2031, which is enough for him to retrain if he starts early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the apprenticeship or the course in the first year. I'd help Hassan sign up for an electrical installation course, because factory automation needs wiring. We'd buy a small flat, but near the pharma cluster, so we'd have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about Hassan dragging his feet, fine about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get Hassan moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a mate lose his job. That's what got him to finally do his driving test. I wish it worked differently, but it's how he is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your learning group at work look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lunchtimes, twice a week, in the canteen. Someone shows how the new packing robot works, and we all have a go on the simulator. Low pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. That's comfortable for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where everyone can make it, if they're sensible. At work I'd still push the learning group. Online I'd be fairly upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'll be a robotics technician long before 2036. Hassan has a decade to move into something hands-on. We'll be fine if we don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, then aim for a senior automation role by 2030. Hassan and I would buy a flat and maybe think about kids around 2030. I'd keep using AI tools every day to stay ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'wasting it' look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Assuming it'll never happen. Lots of people at my plant would say 2036 is ages away and do nothing until 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Does the timeline matter for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd want us both settled in safer jobs first. With ten years, that's doable. With two, I wouldn't even think about it.

I'd keep running the **learning group** at work.
think: I'll be a **robotics technician** long before 2036.

fieldNote: She fears **complacency** among colleagues more than the technology itself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes both our incomes in five years. What would help is paid apprenticeships for adults, not just school leavers, and help for people like Hassan who need a push to move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about couples. Everyone asks about my job, but our household is two jobs, and they're hit at different times. That changes everything about planning.
